name: Proper Noun

dimensions.form: Noun specialized to head proper names; morphologically simple or compound. Normally written with an initial capital, subject to lexical and stylistic exceptions.
dimensions.meaning: Individual-specific, archetypal, institutional, or geographical features
dimensions.function: Head of proper NP; licenses bare NP without determiner
dimensions.distribution: Heads Nom in proper NPs; modifier position in N-N compounds

1.details: Core semantic features characterizing a particular individual

2.details: Characteristic semantic features that can ground metaphorical extension

3.details: Semantic features associated with institutional entities

relatedConstructions.notes: Bidirectional syntax-semantics interface; proper nouns cue proper-name interpretation, proper-name intention licenses proper noun choice
Proper noun formally heads proper NP (via Nom)

projection.target: Proper noun and proper name need not have the same extent. New Zealand is a multiword name, and a noun normally used as a name can appear in an explicitly descriptive NP such as another Einstein.
projection.evidence: CGEL separates the word category from the whole designation and documents secondary uses.

curious.title: Names and the words that make them
curious.summary: A proper noun is a word specialized to serve as the main word of a name, such as Einstein, Waterloo, Harvard or Everest.
curious.body: Einstein, Waterloo, Harvard, Pacific and Everest are all proper nouns. Each is the main word of a name, and each carries associations. Einstein brings to mind a particular person. Waterloo brings to mind defeat, Harvard a university and Everest a mountain. A name can be longer than the word that heads it: New Zealand is a name of more than one word. A word normally used as a name can also appear in a descriptive phrase, as in another Einstein. Proper nouns are normally written with a capital letter, with some exceptions.
curious.try: Think of a name for a person, a place and a group. Which of them could have a descriptive phrase around it, such as another one?

teacher.summary: Separates the proper noun as a word category from the proper name, with secondary uses such as another Einstein.
teacher.explain: A proper noun is a noun specialized to head proper names. It is morphologically simple or compound and normally written with an initial capital, subject to lexical and stylistic exceptions. A proper noun heads a proper noun phrase and can appear without a determiner. In this dictionary, proper noun is a syntactic category and proper name a semantic one, and they need not have the same extent: New Zealand is a multiword name, and a noun normally used as a name can occur in a descriptive phrase such as another Einstein. This dictionary groups features as individual (Einstein), archetypal (Waterloo), institutional (Harvard) and geographical (Pacific, Everest).
teacher.terms: Proper noun is the traditional term and the one used here. This dictionary separates it from proper name, which it treats as a semantic category.

contrasts.note: A multiword name; the proper noun and the name differ in extent.
A name-type noun in a descriptive phrase.

watch_for: A learner might think the capital letter alone makes a word a proper noun.
A learner might treat New Zealand as one word because it is one name.
A learner might think proper noun and proper name are the same category.
teacher.activity: Students list names of people, places and institutions. For each name, they say whether it is a single word or several, and they write one descriptive phrase using a name, such as another one.

child.hook: Why does Kim get a capital letter but dog doesn't?
child.explain: A proper noun is a word used as a name, like Einstein or Everest. New Zealand is one name made of two words. A name normally starts with a capital letter.
child.play: Write names of a person, a pet, a town and a mountain. Circle the capital letters. Which names have more than one word?

checked.note: Fixed: child explain no longer uses the unexplained technical sense of 'heads a name'; it now says a proper noun is a word used as a name, with Einstein and Everest as examples and New Zealand as a two-word name. Also fixed (unflagged): curious summary and body replaced 'heads a name' with 'the main word of a name' for the same reason.
